claims.text: Combined in situ TGA and high-temperature XRD can simultaneously measure real-time oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in multicomponent alloys.
In situ high-temperature XRD can identify time- and temperature-dependent phase formation and transformation during alloy oxidation.
The combined method captures transient oxidation products that conventional ex situ measurements miss.
The starting high-entropy or multi-element alloy has a relatively uniform bulk composition and microstructure.
A high-temperature chamber can be equipped to continuously record both gravimetric mass changes and XRD patterns under controlled oxidizing conditions.
Temperatures from 600 to 1200 °C are representative of relevant alloy service environments.
Transient oxides and stable-phase evolution can be directly observed in real time by high-temperature XRD.
XRD-observed phase evolution can be correlated with TGA mass gains or losses.
In situ data reveal oxidation kinetics and sequential phase transformations.
In situ measurements identify short-lived oxide species that form and subsequently transform at high temperature.
Combining XRD with TGA directly links microstructural evolution to weight changes.
Transitory oxide phases and changes in the underlying alloy structure will be directly observed in real time.
The observed phase changes will correlate precisely with TGA mass changes.
The combined measurements will distinguish oxidation stages that are obscured by ex situ or mass-only measurements.
Conventional TGA combined with ex situ XRD captures only endpoint phase measurements and may miss short-lived intermediate oxides.
The proposed method requires a high-temperature XRD cell coupled with TGA and carefully controlled atmosphere.
Sample geometries or compositions that strongly attenuate or scatter X-rays may be difficult to analyze.
Oxidation products and phase behavior depend on the atmosphere or reactive-gas partial pressure.
The temperature ranges and oxide identities vary among alloy compositions because of element-specific interactions.
